```{r table-styling}
ellipsis <- function(df, nhead=5L, ntail=2) {
    rownames(df) = as.character(1:nrow(df))
    stopifnot("data.frame" %in% class(df))
    els <- rep(NA, ncol(df)) %>% 
        matrix(nrow=1, dimnames=list(NULL, names(df))) %>% 
        data.frame(stringsAsFactors=FALSE) %>% 
        tibble::as_tibble()
    rownames(els) = "⋮"
    dplyr::bind_rows(head(df, nhead), els, tail(df, ntail))
}
```

# Introductory Exercises

## Exercise 1: One Regression Line

- Here's a plot of some data with binary $X$ and $Y$. We've jittered the points a little.

- Hint. What are the means of the  X=1 and X=0 subsamples? What does this tell us?

## Exercise 1: Solution

![](figures/BoundRegMatchPosB){height=600px}

- The slope is $1/3$ ($2/6$). 
- The line goes through the subsample means:
$2/6$ on the left and $4/6$ on the right.
- So it rises by $4/6-2/6=2/6$ as it runs a distance of $1-0=1$.

## Exercise 3: Three Regression Lines

- Now let's make our covariate $Z$ three-valued: $Z \in \{a,b,c\}$.

## Exercise 3: Solution

![](figures/BoundRegMatchNeg){height=600px}

- Let's think about the *average slope* here. 
- There are two averages we might think of...
  - The simple unweighted average, $\frac{1}{3}\sum_z \text{slope}_z$
  - The subsample-size weighted average, $\sum_z P_z \ \text{slope}_z$ for $P_z=N_z/N$.
- Both are negative. And that's interesting---when we drew one line ignoring $z$, the slope was positive.

## Lesson

![](figures/BoundRegMatchNeg){height=600px}

- The *ignore-z slope* is not necessarily similar to the *average-z slope*.
- This has huge implications. People often get confused because they mean one and use the other.
- We'll explore this in some examples soon. Any questions now?

## What Regression Is {.small}

- Regression is *choosing a curve* that predicts outcomes (Y) from covariates (X).
- We choose from a set of curves we call a **regression model**.
- Saying **least squares regression** specifies that we choose the best according to a particular criterion.
- We pick the curve that minimizes the sum of squared errors.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat \mu &= \argmin_{m \in \model} \ell(m) \qfor \ell(m) = \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{m(X_i) - Y_i}^2 \quad \text{ where } \ 
&& \model \ \text{ is the model} \\
&&& m \ \text{ is a curve we're considering } \\
&&& \ell(m) \ \text{ is the criterion we're using to choose} \\
&&& \hat\mu \ \text{ is the curve we do choose}.
\end{aligned}
$$

- We can then use that curve to summarize the data.
- We can make a prediction $Y \approx \hat\mu(X)$ at any value of $X$.
- We can summarize the predictions at multiple values of $X$.
  - e.g. average treatment effects in our gym subsidy example.
  - e.g. average increase in income associated with a year of high school. 
  

## Models for Data With More Than One Covariate

- Often we want to work with subsamples defined in terms of multiple covariates.
- As with continuous covariates, there are many ways to do this.
- And as with continuous covariates, the choice matters: misspecification leads to big problems inferentially.
- Today we will look at two common approaches to modeling data with two covariates.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 z } && \text{ additive model } \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 z + \textcolor{blue}{b_{3} xz} } && \text{ fully-interacted model }
\end{aligned}
$$

- In the *additive model*, the influences of each covariate add together. 
  - This is essentially never how our covariates influence our outcome in reality.
  - So this model is essentially always misspecified. 
- In *fully-interacted model*, the influence of one covariate depends on the value of the other. 
  - The [interaction term]{.fg style="color:blue"} captures this dependence.
  - This isn't misspecified when our covariates are binary. It'll go through the 4 subsample means.
- When we have more than two covariates, these are the extremes---there are models somewhere in between.

##  A Note on Interpretation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\model &= \qty{ m(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 z } && \text{ additive model } \\
\model &= \qty{ m(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 z + \textcolor{blue}{b_{3} xz} } && \text{ fully-interacted model }
\end{aligned}
$$

- Some people focus on the **estimated coefficients** in models like this. In my opinion, this is a mistake.
- These coefficients *are* summaries of our curve $\hat\mu$. But **they're different summaries in different models**.
- It makes sense to think about which model is best if you want to estimate an average treatment effect.
- It doesn't make sense to think about which model is best if you want to estimate *the coefficient of $x$*.
- We saw in our intro exercise that the least squares slopes can be totally different when ...
  - we ignore $z$ 
  - we find different slopes for each $z$ --- even if we then average them.
- My advice: **focus on the curve**. 
  - If someone talks about a coefficient ... 
  - look at their model and see what it does to the curve.

## One Binary and One Continuous Covariate

- Here's what we draw when we have two covariates and ...

## One Binary and One Continuous Covariate

![](figures/em3D1){height=500px}

- But what the math sees is this. It sees points in 3D space.
  - One dimension for the outcome
  - One dimension for the continuous covariate
  - One dimension for the binary covariate. 
- It just happens that all points lie on two sheets---one for each value of the binary covariate.


## One Binary and One Continuous Covariate

![](figures/em3D2){height=500px}

- We can rotate this plot to get a better sense of things.
- That's a useful thing to do with 3D visualization.
- Like you might turn an apple instead of looking at it from a single perspective.

## Regression Plane

![](figures/em3D3){height=500px}


$$
\hat\mu(x,z) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 z
$$

:::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-out data-fragment-index="0"}

- When we take this perspective, the additive regression model *fits a plane* to the data.
- And when $z$ is binary, you can think of this as giving is *two regression lines*
  - One where that plane intersects the sheet with $z=0$ 
  - Another where it intersects the sheet with $z=1$.
:::
::: {.fragment .current-visible data-fragment-index="0"}

- These lines are related because we have to be able to draw a plane through them.
- Using the plane equation---if our geometric intution doesn't do it for us---we can see they have the same slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\mu(x,0) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 \cdot 0 = b_0 + b_1 x \\
\hat\mu(x,1) = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 \cdot 1 = (b_0+b_1) + b_1 x \\
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::::

## Predictions Using Additive Models

$$ m(scscore, dem) = b_0 + b_1 \ \text{scscore} + b_2 \text{dem} $$

- The predicted outcomes for Republican and Democrat-appointed justices with zero SCscore.
$$ \hat\mu(0,0) = \hat\beta_0 \qand \hat\mu(0,1) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_2$$

- The predicted difference in outcomes between Democrat and Republican-appointed justices at $SCscore=s$.
$$ 
\hat \mu(s,1) - \hat \mu(s,0) = \qty(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 s + \hat\beta_2) - \qty(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 s) = \hat\beta_2 \qqtext{ for any } s.
$$

- What is this? And what's weird about it?
$$ \hat\mu(s+1,z)-\hat\mu(s,z)=\hat\beta_1 $$

::: fragment

- It's the predicted difference in outcomes between justices 
  - appointed by the same party (either)
  - and with SCscore $s$ and $s+1$ (for any $s$)
- You might think this should depend on party and $s$, but the model rules out that possibility.

:::
  

# The Fully-Interacted Model


## Breaking Down the Fully Interacted Model
![](figures/pscInt){height=600px}

$$ \hat\mu(scscore, dem) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot \text{scscore} + \hat\beta_2 \cdot \text{dem} + \hat \beta_4  \cdot \text{scscore} \cdot \text{dem} $$

## Breaking Down the Fully Interacted Model
![](figures/pscInt0){height=600px}
$$ \hat\mu(scscore, dem) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot \text{scscore} + \hat\beta_2 \cdot \text{dem} + \hat \beta_4  \cdot \text{scscore} \cdot \text{dem} $$

## Breaking Down the Fully Interacted Model
![](figures/pscInt1){height=600px}
$$ \hat\mu(scscore, dem) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot \text{scscore} + \hat\beta_2 \cdot \text{dem} + \hat \beta_4  \cdot \text{scscore} \cdot \text{dem} $$

## Breaking Down the Fully Interacted Model
![](figures/pscInt2){height=600px}
$$ \hat\mu(scscore, dem) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot \text{scscore} + \hat\beta_2 \cdot \text{dem} + \hat \beta_4  \cdot \text{scscore} \cdot \text{dem} $$

## Breaking Down the Fully Interacted Model
![](figures/pscInt3){height=600px}
$$ \hat\mu(scscore, dem) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot \text{scscore} + \hat\beta_2 \cdot \text{dem} + \hat \beta_4  \cdot \text{scscore} \cdot \text{dem} $$

## Predictions Using The Fully-Interacted Model

$$ m(scscore, dem) = b_0 + b_1 \ \text{scscore} + b_2 \text{dem} + b_3 \text{scscore} \ \text{dem}  $$

- The predicted outcomes for Republican and Democrat-appointed justices with zero SCscore.
$$ \hat\mu(0,0) = \hat\beta_0 \qand \hat\mu(0,1) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_2$$

- The predicted difference in outcomes between Democrat and Republican-appointed justices at $SCscore=s$.
$$ 
\hat \mu(s,1) - \hat \mu(s,0) = \qty(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 s + \hat\beta_2 + \textcolor{blue}{\hat\beta_3 s}) - \qty(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 s) = \hat\beta_2 + \textcolor{blue}{\hat\beta_3 s}
$$

- What's the predicted difference in outcomes for two justices appointed by Democrats with scscores $s+1$ and $s$.

::: fragment

$$ 
\begin{aligned}
\hat\mu(s+1,1)-\hat\mu(s,1)
&= \qty{\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 (s+1) + \hat \beta_2 + \hat \beta_3 (s+1)} 
-\qty{\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 s    + \hat \beta_2 + \hat \beta_3  s} \\
&= (\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_3)\qty{(s+1)-s} = \hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_3
\end{aligned}
$$

- What about Republican-appointees?
  
:::
  
## Going Backward: Interpreting Coefficients

$$\hat\mu(scscore,dem) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \cdot scscore + \hat\beta_2 \cdot dem + \hat \beta_4  \cdot scscore \cdot dem$$

# Omitted Variable Bias

Adding and Removing Covariates in the Additive Model

## Question

![](figures/finalAct2){height=600px}

- Suppose we want the slope coefficient $\hat\beta_1$ from the additive model.
- But we run a regression of $Y$ on $X$ alone. How far off are we?
  
## Starting Point: Residuals and Covariates are Uncorrelated

$$
\hat\beta = \argmin_{\beta \in \R^3} \ell(\beta) \qfor \ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \qty{b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_i - Y_i}^2
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 
&= \frac{\partial}{\partial b_j}\mid_{b=\hat\beta} \ell(b) \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial b_j}\mid_{b=\hat\beta} \qty{b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_i - Y_i}^2 \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n 2 \times \qty{\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 X_i + \hat\beta_2 Z_i - Y_i} \times \frac{\partial}{\partial b_j}\qty{b_0 + b_1 X_i + b_2 Z_i - Y_i}
\end{aligned}
$$

so ...

\begin{align*}
0=\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial b_0}\mid_{b=\hat\beta} &=  -2 \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i  \qfor \hat\varepsilon_i = Y_i - \hat\mu(X_i,Z_i) \\
0=\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial b_1}\mid_{b=\hat\beta} &=  -2 \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i X_i \\
0=\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial b_2}\mid_{b=\hat\beta} &=  -2 \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i Z_i \\
\end{align*}
$$

and therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
0= 0 - 0\bar X &= \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i X_i - \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon \bar X =
\sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon (X_i - \bar X) \\
0= 0 - 0\bar X &= \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon_i X_i - \sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon \bar X =
\sum_{i=1}^n \hat\varepsilon (X_i - \bar X) \\
\end{aligned}
$$

## Deriving A Formula For Omitted Variable Bias




$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) \qty(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 X_i + \hat \beta_2 Z_i + \hat\varepsilon_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&= ...
\end{aligned}
$$

## Deriving A Formula For Omitted Variable Bias

Suppose we want $\hat\beta_1$ from the additive model, but we run a regression
of $Y$ on $X$ alone. How far off are we?

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
&= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) \qty(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 X_i + \hat \beta_2 Z_i + \hat\varepsilon_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&= \hat\beta_0 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2}
+ \hat\beta_1 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) X_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} \\
&+ \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
+ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) \hat\varepsilon_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
\end{aligned}
$$

Here's an expanded version.

- Are any of these terms zero? Why?
- Do we know the values of any of the other sums?

::: fragment
- The first term is zero because $\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \bar X$: $\sum_{i=1}^n \bar X = n \bar X = n \times \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ 
- The last term is zero because the residuals are uncorrelated with $X$: $\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X_i) \hat\varepsilon_i = 0$
- The second term is $\hat\beta_1$ because $\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) X_i = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)X_i - \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) \bar X = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar{X})^2
  - How is this related to what we said about the first term?

:::

## A Formula for Omitted Variable Bias
$$
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2}\\
= \hat \beta_{YX} + \hat\beta_{YZ}\hat\beta_{ZX}
$$

- The first term is the coefficient on $X$ in the additive model.
- The second, which we call **omitted variable bias**, is ...
  - the coefficient on $Z$ 
  - times the coefficient in the simple linear regression of $Z$ on $X$.
- Story: when we leave $Z$ out of our regression, the effect of $Z$ on $Y$ is --- insofar as $X$ predicts $Z$ --- baked into the effect of $X$ in $Y$.
- This is why, if you're discussing coefficients, it's so important to be clear about what model you're using.

## OVB and Covariate Balance

$$
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2}\\
= \hat \beta_{YX} + \hat\beta_{YZ}\hat\beta_{ZX}
$$

- Now we'll use this OVB formula to explain something people do in real experiments that might seem confusing.
  - They look at the coefficient on treatment ($X$) in different models---models that include additional covariates ($X$).  
  - And they act pleased that it's the same. Shouldn't it be different?

- We'll look at an experiment that looked at the effect of various mail treatments on turnout.

## Why doesn't the coefficient on treatment change?
$$
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2} 
=\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2 \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X) Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X)^2}\\
= \hat \beta_{YX} + \hat\beta_{YZ}\hat\beta_{ZX}
$$

::: fragment

- Because treatment $X$ *isn't predictive* of the covariate $Z$.
- We can see from the table that $\hat\beta_{ZX} \approx 0$ so OVB must be zero.

:::

![](figures/GGL.png)


## What We've Left Out

- This is a half-truth. Our OVB formula is for *one omitted covariate* $Z$.
- But what's really getting omitted is many covariates.
- The OVB formula for many covariates is---if we were to try to write it the same way---much more complicated.
- But it looks *exactly like the 1-covariate case* when we use matrix notation.
- Most things do. That's why we use it. We're going to get started now.

# Regression in Matrix Notation

## Scalar vs. Vector Notation

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_1 & = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1 X_{11} + \hat \beta_2 X_{21} + ... \hat \beta_K X_{K1} + \hat\varepsilon_1 \\
Y_2 & = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1 X_{12} + \hat \beta_2 X_{22} + ... \hat \beta_K X_{K2} + \hat\varepsilon_2 \\
& \vdots \\
Y_n & = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1 X_{1n} + \hat \beta_2 X_{2n} + ... \hat \beta_K X_{Kn} + \hat\varepsilon_n \\
\end{aligned}
$$

is just a less compact way of writing ...

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_1 &= \X_{1}^T \hat \beta + \hat\varepsilon_1 \\
Y_2 &= \X_{2}^T \hat \beta + \hat\varepsilon_2 \\
&\vdots \\
Y_n &= \X_{n}^T \hat \beta + \hat\varepsilon_n \\
\end{aligned}
\qfor
\X_i = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ X_{1i} \\ X_{2i} \\ \vdots \\ X_{Ki} \end{pmatrix}
\qand
\hat\beta = \begin{pmatrix} \hat \beta_0 \\ \hat \beta_1 \\ \hat \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \hat \beta_K \end{pmatrix}
$$

## Scalar vs. Matrix Notation

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_1 & = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1 X_{11} + \hat \beta_2 X_{21} + ... \hat \beta_K X_{K1} + \hat\varepsilon_1 \\
Y_2 & = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1 X_{12} + \hat \beta_2 X_{22} + ... \hat \beta_K X_{K2} + \hat\varepsilon_2 \\
& \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad  ... \\
Y_n & = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1 X_{1n} + \hat \beta_2 X_{2n} + ... \hat \beta_K X_{Kn} + \hat\varepsilon_n \\
\end{aligned}
$$

is just a less compact way of writing ...

$$
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\left( \begin{array}{c} Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n \end{array} \right)}_{\Y} 
&=  \underbrace{\left( \begin{array}{ccccc} 1 & X_{11} & X_{21} & ... & X_{K1} \\ 1 & X_{12} & X_{22} & ... & X_{K2} \\ \vdots &  \vdots &  \vdots & \ddots &  \vdots \\  1 & X_{1n} & X_{2n} & ... & X_{Kn} \end{array} \right)}_{\X} 
\underbrace{\left( \begin{array}{c} \hat \beta_0 \\ \hat \beta_1 \\ \hat \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \hat \beta_K \end{array} \right)}_{\hat\beta} 
+ \underbrace{\left( \begin{array}{c} \hat\varepsilon_1 \\  \hat\varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\  \hat\varepsilon_n \end{array} \right)}_{\bf\hat\varepsilon}
\end{aligned}
\Y = \X \hat \beta + {\bf\hat \varepsilon}
$$

i.e., $\Y = \X \hat \beta + {\bf\hat \varepsilon}$.


## Least Squares Solution

$$
\hat\beta  = (\X'\X)^{-1} \X^T \Y \qqtext{solves} 
\argmin_{b \in \R^{K+1}}  \norm{ X b - Y}^2
$$

- Let's prove it. As before, we'll characterize $\hat\beta$ as the vector $b$ where **all partial derivatives are zero**.
- It's easier to do it in **vector notation**. We can convert to **matrix notation** in the end.

$$
\hat\beta = \qty(\sum_{i=1}^n \X_i \X_i^T)^{-1} \sum_i \X_i Y_i  \text{ solves } = \argmin_{b \in \R^{K+1}}  \sum_{i=1}^n  \qty{\X_i^T b - Y_i}^2
$$


## A Simple Summary: A Prediction at a Point x

$$ 
\hat \mu(x) = x^T \hat \beta \qfor \hat\beta  = (\X^T\X)^{-1} \X^T \Y 
$$

- What is the variance of this prediction?

$$
\begin{aligned}
\E \qty{ x^T\hat\beta- \E x^T \hat\beta)}^2 
&=\E \qty{x^T (\hat\beta-\E\hat\beta)}^2 \\ 
&=\E \qty{x^T (\hat\beta-\E\hat\beta)}\qty{(\hat\beta-\E\hat\beta)^T x} \\
&=x^T \qty{\E (\hat\beta-\E\hat\beta) (\hat\beta-\E\hat\beta)^T} x 
\end{aligned}
$$

- Here $\E (\hat\beta-\E\hat\beta) (\hat\beta-\E\hat\beta)^T$ is called 
the **covariance matrix** of $\hat\beta$. 
- And we can calculate it using our formula for $\hat\beta$.

##


## Bias?

- What is the **mean** of this prediction?

$$ 
\hat \mu(x) = x^T \hat \beta \qfor \hat\beta  = (\X^T\X)^{-1} \X^T \Y 
$$
